chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Musa ibn Bakr who said:

Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) said to me: 'The one who seeks this sustenance from its permissible means in order to provide for himself and his family is like the combatant in the way of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.'

So if he is overwhelmed (by poverty), let him borrow upon Allah and upon His Messenger what he can provide for his family with. So if he dies and has not paid it back, it is upon the Imam to pay it. So if he does not pay it, its burden is upon him.
Indeed, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is Saying: 'The charities are only for the poor and the needy, and the officials over them... up to His words: and those in debts.'
So he is the poor, needy, in debt.

key_terms.الْمُجَاهِدِ: The combatant/one striving in the way of God

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on debts incurred for halal family sustenance if the debtor dies?
ai.summary: In this hadith from al-Kafi, Imam al-Rida (AS) elevates the pursuit of lawful sustenance for one's family to the status of jihad, emphasizing that debt incurred for this noble purpose is not a sin but a trust. The text outlines a hierarchical mechanism for debt settlement: if the individual dies, the Imam assumes responsibility for paying it from the public treasury (Bayt al-Mal); if the Imam fails to do so, the spiritual burden remains with him. This ruling underscores the Shia concept of the Imam's financial guardianship and the specific inclusion of the 'debtor' (al-gharimin) as a distinct category of charity recipient, validating the use of zakat for those burdened by legitimate debts.
